uncited: Multi-Pass and Compositing Techniques address the computational complexity and hardware limitations of single-pass direct volume ray casting by decomposing the rendering pipeline into sequential stages .

This family solves the problem of limited shader instruction counts and the lack of conditional fragment discard in early graphics hardware by isolating distinct operations—such as light attenuation, boundary detection, and ray integration—into separate rendering passes .
The concept of image-order compositing was introduced by Marc Levoy in the context of the PIXEL-PLANES 5 hardware, which allowed for efficient per-pixel processing and blending .

The shift toward multi-pass techniques was driven by the architectural constraints of early graphics hardware, specifically the limited number of arithmetic instructions available in fragment shaders and the inability to easily discard fragments based on complex volume traversal logic .
These methods became standard in software renderers and early GPU implementations to achieve high-quality volume rendering without requiring specialized hardware for ray tracing .
